1: # AGENTS.md — 01_Ideas
2: 
3: Raw, unstructured concept capture. Low friction — just enough context to remember.
4: 
5: ## Why have ideas?
6: 
7: To capture every thought about the homelab before it's lost. Ideas are the seed of the pipeline — no idea is too small or too vague.
8: 
9: ## When to create
10: 
11: Any thought about new tech, homelab changes, or wishlist items.
12: 
13: ## Status Lifecycle
14: 
15: ```
16: draft → accepted
17:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/ideas/)
18: ```
19: 
20: - **draft**: Just captured
21: - **accepted**: Worth pursuing
22: - **archived**: Discarded or superseded
23: 
24: ## File system layout
25: 
26: ```
27: 01_Ideas/{topic}/
28: ├── idea-{name}.md     # one per specific idea
29: ├── idea-notes.md      # scratchpad, raw thoughts, links
30: └── overview.md        # high-level summary of the topic area
31: ```
32: 
33: All names in kebab-case. Multiple files per topic allowed. Use the atomic rule (150 lines) to decide when to split.
34: 
35: ## Frontmatter (required)
36: 
37: ```yaml
38: ---
39: title: ""
40: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
41: author: ""
42: date: YYYY-MM-DD
43: tags: []
44: technologies: []
45: related_ideas: []
46: ---
47: ```
48: 
49: Example:
50: 
51: ```yaml
52: ---
53: title: "Move databases to separate node"
54: status: draft
55: author: "padawont"
56: date: 2026-08-13
57: tags: [databases, performance, architecture]
58: technologies: [postgresql, mysql, mariadb]
59: related_ideas: []
60: ---
61: ```
62: 
63: See `./Templates/ideas/idea.md` for a copyable template.
64: 
65: ## Structure
66: 
67: No strict structure — freeform markdown. The template provides a starting point.
68: 
69: ## Conventions
70: 
71: - No formal review needed for `draft → accepted`
72: - No stale timeout — ideas live indefinitely
73: - When `accepted`, the idea is ready — optionally create a Knowledge note
74: - Use `idea-notes.md` for loose thoughts that don't warrant their own file

11: # Run open-weight AI models on local machine
12: 
13: ## Objective
14: 
15: Self-host open-weight LLMs on the local workstation so inference stays local —
16: no API keys, no per-token cost, no data leaving the machine.
17: 
18: ## Current Specs
19: 
20: - CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D — 8C/16T, 3D V-Cache
21: - RAM: 31 GiB total (~24 GiB available)
22: - GPU: AMD Radeon RX 5700 XT (RDNA1, Navi 10) — 8 GiB VRAM, `amdgpu` driver
23: - Disk: 220 GB, 182 GB free
24: - OS: CachyOS Linux, kernel 7.2.6
25: - Runtime: Docker 29.8.1; no ROCm, no NVIDIA tooling
26: 
27: ## Notes
28: 
29: - 8 GiB VRAM fits Q4 7B–8B models; larger models partly offloaded to CPU.
30: - No ROCm on this GPU — RDNA1 support is unofficial, so llama.cpp's Vulkan
31:   backend is the likely path. Ollama is the simplest option.
32: - Runs on this workstation under Docker, not the k3s node.
33: 
34: ## Open Questions
35: 
36: - Which serving stack performs best here: llama.cpp Vulkan or Ollama?

# Expose the NAS only through a zero-trust proxy

## Objective

Reach the NAS from outside the home without opening any inbound ports. Put an
identity-aware proxy in front of every service so each request is authenticated
and authorized before it reaches the NAS. Policy is per-app, not all-or-nothing:
each app gets its own access rule and its own set of allowed identities.
